acv.quote: Two hundred and fifty K ACV.

header.reason: The COO, Halima, decided in one meeting on who would pick up during an on-sale. The competitor brought named people and promised on-call cover, while our tiered support plans struck her as 'a queue with a faster timer'. Jordan believes the load test and the better platform should have won, but the decider only said 'good' to the load test.

findings.label: What started it
findings.finding: Aim messaging at the failed on-sale moment, when payments break minutes in and the incumbent's support only answers after it's over.
findings.quote: Their provider's support was a ticket form. They got a reply after the on-sale was over.

findings.label: Who decided
findings.finding: Coach reps to pitch the operations leader directly on on-sale risk instead of relying on the CTO to relay technical results.
findings.quote: it was Halima's call and she made it in one meeting.

findings.label: The competitor
findings.finding: Pre-empt a named team in the room pitch by bringing the actual account team and stating our on-sale coverage early; Jordan's over-promising theory is an unverified guess.
findings.quote: A named solutions engineer and an account lead, in the room.

findings.label: Our message
findings.finding: Stop answering 'who's my person' with support tiers and response times; answer with the named people and the escalation path.
findings.quote: so it's a queue with a faster timer.

findings.label: Missing proof
findings.finding: Build a written on-sale morning plan showing who's watching, who the customer calls, and what happens at minute four.
findings.quote: She wanted to see, on paper, what we do on an on-sale morning.

findings.label: Their words
findings.finding: Replace uptime-led claims with 'what happens when it's down', 'on-sale morning' and 'someone who picks up' in our ticketing messaging.
findings.quote: I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down.
